passage:
"Two minutes late, and she wants an 'exception'?" Shreya tossed the attendance register onto her bed. "Room 118 gets a week of no late passes."
"A week?" Nazia looked up from her laptop. "Last month you said curfew was a bit much."
"Last month I wasn't on the hostel committee." Shreya pulled on the green committee hoodie. "These first-years think rules are suggestions."
"She said the metro stopped between stations."
"They all have a story. That's why they need to learn."
"We were first-years too."
"And the seniors were strict with us, and we turned out fine." Shreya picked up the whistle. "Honestly, Nazia, some of them deserve it."
Nazia hesitated. "Do they? Or does the hoodie think so?"
"What's that supposed to mean?"
"Nothing." Nazia shut her laptop. "Fine. A week. But I'm not the one telling her."

qa.q: What punishment does Shreya give Room 118?
qa.a: A week of no late passes.

qa.q: What does Shreya's line 'some of them deserve it' show about her thinking?
qa.a: It shows Shreya now feels impatient with the juniors and believes they deserve harshness, a belief that grew after she joined the committee.

qa.q: At which moment could Nazia have changed the outcome, and how?
qa.a: When Nazia asked about the hoodie, she could have pushed on, suggesting they check the metro story or ask the warden, instead of agreeing to a week.

qa.q: How might the first-year in Room 118 feel about a week without late passes?
qa.a: She would likely feel punished for a metro delay she couldn't control, and unheard, since her reason was waved away as 'a story'.

grounding: Two hostel students show a role and hoodie licensing harsh punishment and the belief that juniors deserve it.

passage: I'm Yamini. In my final year I was head marshal for our college's cultural fest, with a neon vest, a lanyard and a walkie-talkie. No teacher checked on us after the first briefing. By day two I was making first-year volunteers redo the chair rows three times 'for discipline', and I shouted at Vaibhav in front of the stage crew for bringing water a minute late. I remember thinking, quite calmly, that the juniors were lazy and needed it. That sentence feels strange to write now. At home I'm the one who lets my cousins cheat at carrom. It was the vest, the walkie-talkie, the fact that nobody asked what we were doing. Months later Vaibhav told me he nearly quit the fest club because of me. I apologised. I'm still working out how easily I became that person.

qa.q: What did Yamini make the first-year volunteers redo?
qa.a: The chair rows, three times 'for discipline'.

qa.q: What did Yamini believe about the juniors during the fest?
qa.a: Yamini thought, quite calmly, that the juniors were lazy and needed it, a thought that now feels strange.

qa.q: What turning point made Yamini face what happened, and what did Yamini do?
qa.a: Months later Vaibhav said he nearly quit the fest club because of Yamini; Yamini apologised and began working out how the role took over.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav experience being shouted at in front of the stage crew?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt humiliated enough that he nearly quit the fest club.

grounding: A student recalls how a vest, a walkie-talkie and no oversight led them to treat junior volunteers harshly and think they deserved it.

passage:
Warden's note, 22 Sept. Vasudha Menon.
Parul (20, second year) was made mess monitor in July. Early on she was fair and even joked with the first-years. Over the past weeks I have watched her change. She now stands at the mess door with the monitor's register and turns back juniors who arrive two minutes late, even when food is left. Tonight she made a first-year, Rinku, wait outside while the others ate, and when I asked why, she said, 'They take advantage otherwise, ma'am. They need to learn.' She believed it. The juniors now go silent when she passes.
What I did next: I spoke with Parul privately and asked how she would have felt last year. I changed the rule so monitors report lateness to me instead of turning anyone away, and I'll rotate the role monthly.

qa.q: What did Parul make the first-year do tonight?
qa.a: Parul made a first-year, Rinku, wait outside while the others ate.

qa.q: What does 'They need to learn' show about what Parul has come to believe?
qa.a: Parul has come to believe the juniors deserve harsh treatment, and feels confident it is right.

qa.q: What changes did Vasudha choose, and why do they help?
qa.a: Vasudha had monitors report lateness instead of turning anyone away and will rotate the role monthly, adding a check and limiting how long one person holds the power.

qa.q: How do the juniors seem to experience Parul now?
qa.a: The juniors seem wary of Parul, going silent whenever she passes.

grounding: A warden records a hostel senior growing harsh as mess monitor and believing juniors deserve it, then adds checks.

passage:
Wednesday night

Orientation committee, week two. We seniors run the 6 am roll call for first-years in the hostel courtyard. The warden set the time but left the rest to us. Committee T-shirts, whistles, a register.

Today Ritu was late for the third time. Four minutes. She said her alarm didn't ring. I took her phone for the night and made her read the hostel rules aloud to everyone. She stood there in her night suit with her voice cracking.

Honestly, she deserved it. These juniors think hostel is a holiday. Last year I was the one being shouted at and I learned.

When I gave the phone back just now, she said "Thank you, didi" very quietly, not looking at me. It bothered me for a second. Then I thought, that's respect. That's how it should be.

Nobody checks what we do in that courtyard. Maybe that's why it works.
- Kalyani

qa.q: How late was Ritu for the roll call today?
qa.a: She was four minutes late.

qa.q: What does Kalyani believe about Ritu and the other juniors?
qa.a: She believes they deserve harsh treatment because they think hostel is a holiday, and she takes Ritu's quiet thanks as respect.

qa.q: What went wrong in how the courtyard roll call was run, and what could fix it?
qa.a: With T-shirts, whistles and no one checking, the seniors punished at will; the warden could set clear limits and check the roll call personally.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt reading the rules aloud with her voice cracking?
qa.a: Ritu likely felt humiliated and afraid, which explains why she thanked her senior quietly without looking at her.

grounding: A hostel senior on an orientation committee enforces rules harshly on a junior because the role allows it, and comes to believe the junior deserves it.

passage: In my third year, I was made floor senior in the girls' hostel in Pune, and I'm embarrassed about how I behaved. I'm Aadhya. The warden gave us a register and said, "Keep the juniors in order." So we did. We did surprise room checks at midnight. We confiscated kettles and made first-years stand in the corridor for ten minutes if they were late. Sonali, a first-year, came back five minutes late from the library once, and I made her write an apology in front of everyone. She cried. I remember thinking, they need to learn. They're careless. I really believed she deserved it. Nobody checked us; the warden trusted us completely. Only later, when my younger sister went to hostel and was treated the same way, did I understand how it felt from below.

qa.q: How late was Sonali from the library?
qa.a: Sonali came back five minutes late.

qa.q: What was Aadhya thinking when Sonali cried?
qa.a: Aadhya felt justified, cold and superior, believing the juniors were careless and deserved it.

qa.q: What could have kept the floor seniors from becoming harsh?
qa.a: The warden could have checked how seniors used the register, and juniors could have had a way to complain.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt writing the apology in front of everyone?
qa.a: Sonali likely felt humiliated and frightened, punished harshly for being five minutes late.

grounding: A former hostel senior recalls enforcing rules harshly on juniors because the role licensed it, believing they deserved it, with no one checking.

passage:
Faculty adviser's note, college fest, day two.
Farhan (third year) is one of the student volunteers on gate security. On day one he was friendly. Today I watched him shout at a first-year for not having his ID ready, make two others empty their bags on the ground, and laugh when one student's papers blew away. He's wearing the black volunteer T-shirt and a lanyard, and he seems to feel it gives him permission. When I asked, he said, "These juniors think they can do anything. They need to be taught." Few people are supervising the volunteers. I've asked Gopika from the organising team to rotate gate duty every two hours and to pair each volunteer with a faculty member. I'll also talk to Farhan tomorrow about what he'd accept if he were the one at the gate.

qa.q: What did Farhan make two students do?
qa.a: He made two others empty their bags on the ground.

qa.q: What does Farhan's comment "They need to be taught" suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Farhan felt superior and justified, believing the juniors deserved harsh treatment.

qa.q: Why is rotating gate duty and pairing volunteers with faculty a good fix?
qa.a: It adds checks and breaks up the role's power, so volunteers are less likely to drift into cruelty.

qa.q: How might the first-year whose papers blew away have felt?
qa.a: The first-year likely felt humiliated and powerless, laughed at by someone in charge.

grounding: A student volunteer in a security role enforces rules harshly on juniors because the role licenses it and few people check, and comes to believe they deserve it.

Friday night
Mess committee duty again. I was in charge of the breakfast line. The rule is no seconds before 8:30. Afreen, a first-year, took a second paratha at 8:20. I made her put it back in front of the whole line. She said she had a practical at nine and hadn't eaten dinner. I said, "Rules are rules." Honestly, the juniors this year are so entitled. They need to learn.
But writing this down, I'm wondering. Last year when I was a first-year, I did the same thing and the committee girl let me keep it. I was so grateful. Now I'm the one with the badge and I didn't even hesitate. When did that happen? Is it the badge? Or was I always like this?
Maybe I'll find Afreen tomorrow.
- Mahima

qa.a: Mahima feels uneasy and doubtful, starting to question whether the badge has made the harshness easy.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt putting the paratha back?
qa.a: Afreen likely felt embarrassed and hungry, humiliated in front of the whole line before her practical.

passage:
At the temple fair in the small town of Hosur, the college's volunteer group wore orange caps and managed the queue for darshan. Kashish and Chaitanya were in charge of the women's line.
By the second day, they had become different. Kashish shouted at an old woman who stepped out of line to sit down. "Back! Rules are rules!" Chaitanya pulled a village boy by the collar for cutting in.
"These people never follow anything," Kashish said at lunch. "They need to be told."
Chaitanya nodded, then paused. "At home, I'd give my seat to that old woman."
Kashish didn't answer. She took off her orange cap and looked at it.

qa.q: What colour were the volunteers' caps?
qa.a: They wore orange caps.

qa.q: What might Kashish be feeling when she takes off her orange cap and looks at it?
qa.a: She seems uneasy and doubtful, starting to notice how the cap made her treat people harshly.

qa.q: What small step could the volunteers take for the rest of the fair?
qa.a: They could treat people the way they would at home, such as helping the old woman sit down, and check each other when they get harsh.

qa.q: How might the old woman who needed to sit feel when Kashish shouts?
qa.a: She would likely feel frightened and humiliated, scolded by a young stranger for resting.

grounding: Shows volunteers at a fair enforcing rules harshly on older and poorer people because the role allows it, and coming to believe they deserve it.

passage:
At the university residence in Uppsala, Ingrid and Yosef were made hall assistants in their second year. They got keys, a clipboard and the right to write warnings.
First-years were loud. By October, Ingrid was writing warnings for a laugh after ten. Yosef took a first-year's speaker away for a week because the student argued.
"They're children," Ingrid said. "They have to learn."
One evening Yosef saw a first-year crying in the kitchen over a warning letter. The student was homesick and had only been playing music from home.
Yosef stood in the doorway, clipboard in hand. Last year that had been him.

qa.q: What did Yosef take away from a first-year?
qa.a: He took a first-year's speaker away for a week.

qa.q: What does Yosef feel, standing in the doorway with the clipboard?
qa.a: He feels shaken and guilty, remembering that last year he was the homesick first-year.

qa.q: What could Ingrid and Yosef change?
qa.a: They could talk to first-years before writing warnings, ask a hall supervisor to review hard cases, and treat them as people, not problems.

qa.q: How does Ingrid see the first-years?
qa.a: Ingrid sees them as children who deserve harsh rules, not as people with reasons like homesickness.

grounding: Shows student hall assistants given keys and warnings who start enforcing rules harshly on first-years and believing they deserve it.

passage: In the engineering hostel, Tarun had been made discipline in-charge for the fresher block, with a register and a key to the gate. The job was only to note late arrivals. But by the second month he was locking the gate at 10:01 sharp and making latecomers stand outside while he lectured them. When Asif, a fresher, came in at 10:05 from the library, Tarun made him wait twenty minutes in the rain. 'Rules are rules. These first-years need to learn.' He noticed he no longer felt bad about it. They were lazy, weren't they? That's what he told his roommates. He didn't notice that last year, as a fresher, he had come in late from the library too. The warden, passing on his round, unlocked the gate himself and asked Tarun to come to his office in the morning.

qa.q: How long did Tarun make Asif wait?
qa.a: Twenty minutes in the rain.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel about making latecomers wait by the second month?
qa.a: Tarun felt justified, even smug, and no longer bad about it, believing the freshers were lazy and deserved it.

qa.q: What could the hostel change to prevent this kind of role drift?
qa.a: Keep the role limited to noting arrivals, with the warden checking regularly, and give freshers a way to complain.

qa.q: How might Asif feel waiting in the rain?
qa.a: Asif likely felt humiliated and resentful, punished for coming back from the library.

grounding: A hostel senior given a small guard-like role enforces it harshly on freshers and comes to believe they deserve it.

passage:
Dear Yash,
Since you start college next month, I want to tell you something I'm not proud of. At our fest in March, I was a volunteer with the red security T-shirt and a walkie-talkie. We were told to keep first-years out of the backstage area. By the second day I was shouting at them, checking their bags when there was no need, making one girl cry because she had come to find her friend. I told myself they were careless kids who needed control. The strange thing is, I felt powerful and right the whole time. It was only on the last night, when I took the T-shirt off, that I thought: would I ever talk to anyone like that in normal clothes? No. If they give you a role like that, remember: the T-shirt isn't you.
Love,
Aparna Didi

qa.q: What was Aparna told to keep first-years out of?
qa.a: The backstage area.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel while shouting at the first-years?
qa.a: Aparna felt powerful and smug, sure of being in the right and believing they were careless kids who needed control.

qa.q: What advice does Aparna give Yash?
qa.a: To remember, if given a role like that, that the T-shirt isn't him, and to treat people as he would in normal clothes.

qa.q: How might the girl who came to find her friend have felt?
qa.a: She likely felt frightened and humiliated, made to cry for doing nothing wrong.

grounding: A young woman's letter admits how a fest security role licensed her to treat first-years harshly and believe they deserved it.

passage: You asked about being a teaching assistant. I'm Harish, and I'll be honest: it brought out something ugly. They gave me a badge and the power to mark first-year lab records. By week five I was tearing up records for a missing date, making juniors redo whole experiments for one smudge. Vandana, a first-year, once asked why her record was marked zero, and I said, 'Because I said so,' and enjoyed it when she flinched. I actually believed they were lazy and needed breaking in. My professor saw the zero, checked the record and called me in. 'Harish, would you treat your cousin like this?' That question stayed with me. I rechecked every record I'd failed. Most were fine. I apologised to Vandana. The badge didn't make me cruel. But it made cruelty feel like my job.

qa.q: What did Harish tear up records for?
qa.a: A missing date.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when Vandana flinched?
qa.a: Harish enjoyed it, feeling powerful and sure the juniors deserved it.

qa.q: What did the professor do that helped Harish change?
qa.a: Checked the record and asked whether Harish would treat a cousin like this, which made the juniors people again.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt when her record was marked zero?
qa.a: Vandana likely felt hurt and unfairly treated, flinching at a senior's harsh reply.

grounding: A young teaching assistant describes how a badge and marking power let him treat juniors harshly and believe they deserved it.

passage:
Day 1 of the college fest, February. Mehak gets a yellow armband: Volunteer, Discipline. She laughs with Leela, "I feel like a traffic cop." She gently waves first-years off the stage steps.
Day 2. A first-year girl sits on the barricade to see better. Mehak yanks her sleeve. "Down. Now. Can't you read?" The girl apologises; Mehak takes her fest pass anyway. Later, to Leela: "They're so entitled, these first-years."
Day 4, after the fest. Leela shows Mehak a video from Day 2: Mehak shouting, the girl in tears, the barricade actually quite sturdy. "That wasn't the Mehak I know," Leela says quietly. Mehak starts to argue that the first-years deserved it, then stops, the armband still in her bag.

qa.q: What did Mehak's armband say?
qa.a: Volunteer, Discipline.

qa.q: Why does Mehak call the first-years "entitled" on Day 2?
qa.a: In the role she felt irritated and powerful, so she began to believe the juniors deserved harsh treatment instead of feeling sorry for the girl.

qa.q: What could Mehak do after seeing the video?
qa.a: She could return the girl's fest pass, apologise, and ask the organisers for clear limits on what volunteers may do.

qa.q: What was it like for the first-year on the barricade?
qa.a: It was frightening and humiliating to be shouted at and lose the pass for trying to see the stage, even after apologising.

grounding: A student volunteer given a discipline armband enforces rules harshly on a junior and comes to believe the juniors deserve it.
